title: Capstone: one monitor, several interacting guarantees

opening.title: Make several promises hold at once
keyPoints: Normalize mixed units before judging them
Commit complete batches or preserve old history
Replace future policy without rewriting past decisions
Dr. Charles Dorner
opening.narration: The capstone is a workshop temperature monitor built from the earlier lessons. The important challenge is not recognizing three pattern names. It is making several promises hold together. Values arrive in two units, rules may change between batches, rejected batches must leave no partial history, and reports must remember decisions made at intake. We will ask which boundary protects each promise, then follow one request across them. This is a teaching program with supplied in-memory values. It does not read real sensors or control a heater. Its deliberately small scope lets us inspect every state change and test an exact report without hiding behind external devices.

question.prompt: What makes an integration correct beyond each small component working alone?
question.answer: The components must agree on shared contracts, including units, ordering, state, ownership, failure behavior, and the meaning of stored history.

opening.title: Turn the job into an explicit contract
keyPoints: Positive identifiers increase across the whole session
Temperatures normalize to −40 through 125 °C
At most eight accepted readings
Ingest only while running; replace only idle or paused
opening.narration: Before choosing classes, write the limits. Every identifier must be positive and greater than the last accepted identifier, including earlier items in the same batch. Accepted Celsius temperatures must lie between minus forty and one hundred twenty-five, with both endpoints allowed. The monitor holds at most eight records. A batch can be admitted only in the running state, and a rule can be replaced only while idle or paused. Stopped is final for this monitor object. These rules are not claims about all real sensors; they define this program. They give us concrete questions to ask of conversion, policy, state methods, and commit behavior.

question.prompt: Can a batch with identifiers 4 and 4 be accepted after an existing history ending at 3?
question.answer: No. The second identifier fails the strictly increasing rule within the same batch, so the entire batch must leave history unchanged.

opening.title: The simplest comparison can answer the wrong question
keyPoints: A threshold of 80 means 80 °C
100 °F is about 37.8 °C
A valid numeric comparison can use the wrong unit
opening.narration: The first small design compares a number to eighty and prints a label. That works if every number is already valid Celsius. When one hundred arrives tagged Fahrenheit, the same branch prints ALERT even though the normalized temperature is about thirty-seven point eight Celsius. The compiler sees two numbers and a valid comparison. It cannot infer the missing physical meaning. This complete demonstration prints both decisions so the error is visible. The repair is to normalize before classifying. We use decimal constants in the conversion so division has floating-point meaning, and we present one decimal place only for display, not as an extra rounding step before the decision.
actions: Predict the three printed lines before running the program.
Ask which wrong assumption is present even though every C++ expression is valid.

opening.title: One normalization boundary prevents three local guesses
keyPoints: RawSample still carries an outside unit tag
Sample carries a field named celsius
Rules and reports consume the internal representation
opening.narration: Suppose ingest, a report tool, and a replay tool each copy the conversion formula. The next unit change now requires three edits, and each caller might handle an unknown tag differently. SampleAdapter earns its place by making one boundary responsible for converting and validating outside values. RawSample includes an identifier, a number, and a unit character. Sample includes the identifier and a field named celsius. That field name carries a useful internal promise. This capstone uses Adapter’s translation responsibility as a value-conversion helper. It does not reproduce an inheritance-based Target and wrapped Adaptee structure merely to make the diagram look more elaborate.

question.prompt: Why is naming the internal field celsius stronger than calling it value?
question.answer: It makes the representation contract visible to later code, reducing the chance that rules or reports silently interpret the same number in different units.

opening.title: Rejecting a request is not the same as rolling it back
keyPoints: Direct mutation can leave the first item behind
A private candidate keeps live history unchanged
Publish the candidate only after every item passes
opening.narration: Here we isolate the batch problem using integer identifiers rather than the full monitor. The history begins with ten, and the proposed batch contains eleven followed by an invalid zero. The direct version appends eleven before throwing, so its count becomes two. The staged version copies the old history, changes only the copy, and swaps after the whole batch passes. Because zero causes an exception first, the live count stays one. Catching the exception did not undo the direct append. The guarantee comes from where mutation occurs. This simplified program models the capstone’s commit design without adding units, policies, or states yet.
actions: Mark the first live mutation in each version.
Predict both counts, then run and explain why the catch blocks are not rollback mechanisms.

question.prompt: Why does catching the same error leave different counts?
question.answer: The direct version has already mutated live history. The staged version changed only a local candidate, which is destroyed when the exception leaves the function.

opening.title: Each structure must pay for one requirement
keyPoints: Adapter normalizes the external representation
Strategy varies the future alert decision
Facade centralizes a report request
An enum handles this small lifecycle
opening.narration: Now we can justify the main boundaries. Mixed units motivate adaptation. Replaceable alert rules motivate Strategy: Monitor owns an AlertRule and calls alert without inspecting the concrete rule type. Repeated report construction motivates ReportFacade, which gathers stored rows, counts alerts, and formats one result. The lifecycle needs explicit states and guarded transitions, but not a class for every state. This distinction matters in a capstone: integrating lessons means selecting useful structures and explaining deliberate omissions. A private staged vector provides exception safety; it is not automatically Command or Memento. A suggestive class name or a familiar arrow is never enough to establish a pattern’s mechanism.

mechanism.title: Reject invalid numbers before ordinary range checks
keyPoints: Reject nonpositive identifiers
Reject nonfinite raw and converted values
Only C and F are accepted unit tags
Range comparisons alone do not reject NaN
mechanism.narration: A finite value is an ordinary bounded number, rather than infinity or NaN, which means not a number. NaN is an important trap: both a less-than comparison and a greater-than comparison against ordinary limits are false. An implementation that only asks whether a value is below minus forty or above one hundred twenty-five may therefore let NaN pass. SampleAdapter first uses std::isfinite on the incoming number, then validates the converted result as well. Very large finite arithmetic can overflow to infinity during conversion. Unknown tags are rejected rather than guessed. These checks establish the assumptions that alert rules and reports rely on later.
actions: Ask learners to state the relevant invariant before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Why does checking c < −40 or c > 125 not fully validate c?
question.answer: For NaN both comparisons are false. The implementation must also reject nonfinite values with std::isfinite.

mechanism.title: Thresholds and tolerances are written policy
keyPoints: AtLeast uses an inclusive ≥ comparison
OutsideBand later treats both endpoints as acceptable
Conversion uses floating-point operands
Do not add an unexplained epsilon
mechanism.narration: The first rule, AtLeast, marks a reading when its Celsius value is greater than or equal to the stored limit. The equal case is part of the contract, so eighty Celsius at a limit of eighty is an alert. A different policy may use different endpoint behavior; the later OutsideBand extension allows its low and high endpoints. For conversion, five divided by nine with integer operands would be zero, so the real source uses decimal constants and a visible operation order. Real instruments may need a tolerance near a physical limit, but that is a separate written policy. An unexplained epsilon changes which values the program admits or classifies.

question.prompt: If someone changes AtLeast from >= to >, which small test exposes the regression?

mechanism.title: The rule’s signature carries several different promises
keyPoints: const Sample& borrows one normalized sample
Trailing const restricts changes through the rule object
virtual dispatch selects the current concrete rule
noexcept does not mean “cannot be wrong”
mechanism.narration: Read the rule declaration one piece at a time. The result is bool, a true-or-false decision. const Sample ampersand borrows the normalized sample and prevents changing it through this parameter. The const after the parameter list limits ordinary changes to the rule through the call. virtual permits dispatch through the base interface, and a concrete rule uses override to check the match at compile time. noexcept promises that an exception will not escape the operation. It does not prove that the implementation returns the correct answer or has no outside effects. If an exception escapes a noexcept function, the program terminates rather than producing an ordinary rejected batch.
actions: Ask learners to state the relevant invariant before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Can ingest catch an exception that escapes a noexcept AlertRule::alert and then safely roll back?
question.answer: No. An exception escaping that noexcept operation triggers termination. Ordinary exception rollback is not a recovery plan for a rule that violates this contract.

mechanism.title: Local rollback cannot undo an outside side effect
keyPoints: AtLeast only compares values
An external counter or message would escape staging
Future stateful policies need a reviewed transaction boundary
mechanism.narration: Staging protects records_, but it cannot unsend a message. Imagine a future rule increments an external alert counter before a later sample in the batch fails conversion. The live history rolls back, yet the counter has already changed. Even a const noexcept member function could perform such an outside effect through an alias or external service. That is why the capstone’s rule contract also requires judging a sample to have no outside side effects. AtLeast satisfies this by comparing two values. If a later policy truly needs history or notification, design that new responsibility explicitly and decide when its effects become committed.

question.prompt: Does a const noexcept signature alone prove the batch has no external side effects?
question.answer: No. The behavioral contract must forbid those effects, and implementations must be reviewed and tested against it.

mechanism.title: Four names eliminate impossible flag combinations
keyPoints: idle → running on start
running ↔ paused on pause/resume
running or paused → stopped on stop
No transition leaves stopped
mechanism.narration: Three booleans such as started, paused, and stopped create combinations that may have no sensible meaning. A finite-state machine uses one named state and a table of permitted changes instead. The source begins idle, starts running, may pause and resume, and can stop from either active state. Stopped is final for that object. Each method checks the old state before assigning the new state, so an invalid call leaves the old state intact. This is an enum-based state machine, not the polymorphic State pattern. Four short gates do not justify separate state objects; larger independent state behavior might change that decision later.

question.prompt: What should resume do while the monitor is idle?
question.answer: Reject the request with logic_error and leave the state idle. It must not repair the caller’s mistake by silently starting.

mechanism.title: Empty input still obeys the operation’s state contract
keyPoints: An empty batch is a no-op only while running
State is checked before processing elements
Stopped stays final even for an empty batch
mechanism.narration: An empty batch can tempt an implementer to return immediately before checking anything else. In this program, that would break the public contract. Ingest is a running-state operation, so even an empty batch must be rejected while idle, paused, or stopped. While running, it is allowed and adds nothing. This example shows why edge cases should be judged against the whole operation rather than only the loop body. A different application could define empty input as universally harmless, but it would be a different contract. The source’s order of checks makes its chosen meaning clear and testable.

question.prompt: Why is `if (batch.empty()) return;` before the state check incorrect here?
question.answer: It would accept ingest calls in states where ingest is forbidden, including stopped. Empty input does not waive the state precondition.

mechanism.title: Trace ingestion as a sequence of protected boundaries
keyPoints: Check state and capacity before staging
Convert each raw item to a Sample
Compare against the last staged identifier
Classify, append privately, then commit once
mechanism.narration: Follow the actual order, because a reordered check can change behavior. Ingest first rejects the wrong state and excess capacity. It then copies accepted records into staged. For each raw item, conversion establishes a valid Celsius Sample. The identifier must exceed the last staged identifier, not merely the last identifier from the old history. That catches duplicates introduced earlier in this same batch. The current rule classifies the normalized sample, and a Record containing both the sample and its decision is appended privately. Only a fully completed loop reaches the final swap. At every earlier rejection, accepted history remains the same.

question.prompt: Why compare against staged.back() instead of only records_.back()?
question.answer: The staged history includes earlier items from the current batch, so it detects duplicates and decreasing identifiers within that batch.

mechanism.title: The commit point is a small operation with a large meaning
keyPoints: Before swap: records_ is the old accepted history
After swap: records_ is the complete new history
The local staged vector then destroys old storage
This is a scoped strong exception guarantee
mechanism.narration: The commit point is the operation that makes the prepared change visible as accepted state. Here records_.swap(staged) exchanges the vectors after every item has passed. With the standard allocator used in this source, vector swap is nonthrowing. Before that line, records_ still holds the old history; after it, records_ holds the entire new history. The local staged vector now owns the old storage and releases it as the function ends. If copying, conversion, ordering checks, or appending throws earlier, local cleanup discards the candidate. This is the strong exception guarantee for stored history under ordinary C++ exception flow, not durable recovery from a process crash.

theory.what: A private candidate followed by one nonthrowing swap gives the history a single publication point.
theory.where: Monitor::ingest, after the loop has converted and checked every item.
theory.why: A rejected batch must not leave a valid prefix of that batch in accepted history.
theory.invariant: Observable accepted history is either the old history or the complete accepted new history.
theory.risk: External side effects, contract-violating rules, termination, and process crashes are outside this local exception guarantee.

mechanism.title: Capacity arithmetic relies on an earlier invariant
keyPoints: Accepted history never exceeds eight records
Compute spare capacity as cap minus current size
Compare batch size to spare capacity
Do not silently drop excess readings
mechanism.narration: The capacity check compares the incoming batch size with cap minus the current number of records. That subtraction is safe because the monitor already preserves the invariant that accepted history never exceeds eight records. Unsigned subtraction would be dangerous if that invariant were not true: a value below zero could wrap to a very large result. The check rejects the whole oversized batch before staging. It does not accept the first few readings or discard the rest. This is another place where a local line relies on a wider guarantee. When increasing capacity or adding a bulk-import path, preserve that guarantee at every entry point.
actions: Ask learners to state the relevant invariant before revealing the answer.

mechanism.title: The monitor owns one rule and rejects a missing one
keyPoints: unique_ptr makes the owning relationship explicit
Construction establishes a usable rule
Replacement checks state and null before assignment
Virtual destruction reaches the concrete rule
mechanism.narration: Monitor receives an owning unique_ptr by value and moves it into its rule_ member. The constructor rejects a missing rule, so a successfully constructed monitor has a usable policy. Replacement also checks the allowed state and the proposed pointer before assigning. If either check fails, the current member remains valid. The incoming parameter itself owns the proposed replacement during the call, so it is cleaned up if the call rejects it. On successful assignment, the old member-owned rule is destroyed. AlertRule’s virtual destructor makes deletion through the base owning pointer reach the concrete destructor correctly. These are lifetime facts, not merely class-diagram relationships.

question.prompt: If a paused monitor receives replace_rule(nullptr), what must remain true afterward?
question.answer: The request is rejected and the monitor still owns its previous valid rule; the non-null invariant must not be lost.

mechanism.title: A stable session identity can justify deleting move
keyPoints: Monitor copying and moving are compile-time errors
A default move could empty the source rule owner
The moved-from source might still say running
Moving an owning handle is a different operation
mechanism.narration: It may seem natural to let every modern C++ type move, but the monitor’s invariant makes that choice nontrivial. An automatic move could transfer rule_ out of the source while leaving its state_ equal to running. Calling ingest on that moved-from source could then follow an empty pointer. This source chooses a simpler contract: a Monitor object has a stable identity and cannot be copied or moved. The deleted operations and static assertions enforce that at compile time. Moving a unique_ptr that owns a Monitor would transfer the handle without moving the Monitor object itself. Those are different operations with different effects on invariants.

question.prompt: Why does “unique_ptr is movable” not automatically mean this Monitor should be movable?
question.answer: Moving its member could invalidate the source Monitor’s non-null rule invariant while leaving the source callable. The whole object needs its own explicit move contract.

mechanism.title: A vector reference and an element reference have different risks
keyPoints: records() borrows the vector object
A commit can replace the vector’s element storage
Do not keep element references or iterators across ingest
The report finishes its short borrow before mutation
mechanism.narration: The records accessor returns a const reference to the vector object stored inside Monitor. That vector object continues to exist while the monitor lives, even when its contents are swapped. A reference to one element is different. Ingest can swap out the old storage, which is then destroyed with staged, so an old element reference or iterator may become invalid. The report avoids this trap by borrowing only for the duration of summary and returning an independent string. This is single-threaded code: const access does not supply synchronization. Adding concurrent reporting and ingestion requires a separate decision about locking or snapshots.

question.prompt: After ingest commits, why can a retained reference to records_ remain valid while a retained reference to its former first Record does not?
question.answer: The vector member object still exists, but its former element storage has been swapped out and destroyed. Object identity and element lifetime are different.

mechanism.title: The report presents accepted history, not a new policy run
keyPoints: Borrow stored records and count their saved flags
Return owned text with stable formatting
Classic locale fixes formatting conventions
A free function is a reasonable small alternative
mechanism.narration: ReportFacade gathers the report request into one operation. It borrows the monitor, traverses stored records, counts saved alert flags, and builds an independent string. The string uses a classic locale and one digit after the decimal point so the expected report does not depend on ordinary machine formatting settings. It does not run the current strategy over old readings. That distinction preserves the report’s meaning as a record of intake decisions. A free function could reasonably provide the same small facade boundary; the static class form is not the core benefit. The useful contract is one stable request with a clear owned result and a short, safe borrow.

closing.title: History records what was decided then
keyPoints: 80 °C arrived under an inclusive 80 °C rule
The new rule uses 100 °C
Saved history stays alert; a new 90 °C reading is ok
closing.narration: This small program separates historical data from a current calculation. One record stores eighty Celsius and the true decision made under an eighty-degree limit. After the limit becomes one hundred, re-running the old value would produce false, but that is not what happened at intake. The program prints one saved alert, zero incorrectly recomputed old alerts, and no alert for a future ninety-degree reading. Both comparisons are mathematically valid. The difference is the question being answered. A report of past decisions must preserve its saved flags; a what-if analysis under today’s policy can be offered separately without silently rewriting history.

closing.title: OutsideBand is an extension of the decision boundary
keyPoints: Require finite −40 ≤ low ≤ high ≤ 125
Alert below low or above high
Both endpoints remain acceptable
Keep Monitor and its old checks unchanged
closing.narration: The lab asks for a second kind of AlertRule called OutsideBand. It accepts two finite Celsius limits in order and marks readings strictly below the low limit or strictly above the high limit. For the band twenty through sixty, the readings nineteen, twenty, sixty, and sixty-one should give alert, ok, ok, alert. A zero-width band is valid: exactly its one endpoint is acceptable. The existing virtual alert request already expresses this decision, so Monitor need not change. Preserve all earlier checks and add tests for construction failures, endpoints, late batch rejection, replacement back to AtLeast, and unchanged old flags. That is useful extension evidence, not merely an extra subclass.

question.prompt: What comparisons preserve acceptable endpoints for OutsideBand?

closing.title: Find the earliest broken promise, not the last symptom
keyPoints: Record the state, count, last identifier, and current rule
Trace normalization before classification
Locate the first live mutation
Compare the complete report before and after rejection
closing.narration: Suppose a bad batch adds a fourth row even though the call reports an unknown unit. Do not start by changing the error message. Write the old state and complete report, then follow the first item through conversion, classification, and append. If it reaches records_ before the second item fails, the first broken promise is partial mutation before full acceptance. For another failure, an eighty-degree row loses its alert after replacement; that points to re-evaluating saved history. Debugging the earliest broken promise narrows the search more effectively than examining only the final incorrect count. Keep a failing test that captures the whole visible effect of the defect.

closing.title: Different checks protect different parts of the contract

Runtime checks cover values, state, and exact report
Lifetime probes observe destruction through valid borrows
A passing suite has a stated scope
closing.narration: The source uses compile-time type-trait assertions to verify that Monitor cannot be copied or moved. Running checks then test value rules, state transitions, rollback, rule replacement, and exact report text. The check helper throws when a condition is false, so these checks do not disappear when a release build defines NDEBUG, unlike ordinary assert. LifetimeRule changes a borrowed flag when destroyed; the flag remains alive around the monitored scope, making the observation valid. The rejects helper expects a logic_error-family exception. These tests exercise specified cases. They do not exhaust allocator failures, all numeric inputs, concurrency, or crash recovery, so report their evidence with those limits.

closing.title: A small capacity makes staging affordable; growth changes the cost
keyPoints: For n stored and b new: work is proportional to n + b
Temporary storage is also proportional to n + b
Repeated single inserts into an unbounded history can accumulate quadratic copying
Choose a new transaction design from measured workloads
closing.narration: Copying accepted history makes the exception guarantee easy to inspect, and eight records make its cost tightly bounded. With n existing records and b new ones, staging and processing require work and temporary storage proportional to n plus b. Now imagine removing the cap and ingesting one reading at a time. The successive copies grow as one, two, three, and so on; total work can become quadratic in the final history size. That does not make today’s bounded design wrong. It identifies a future pressure. A journal, chunked storage, or separately validated batch might help, but each needs a new proof of ordering, ownership, and commit behavior.
actions: Ask learners to state the relevant invariant before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Why is “remove cap = 8” more than a harmless constant change for a large deployment?
question.answer: It can expose repeated full-history copies as a major time and memory cost. The workload and commit strategy need review while preserving the existing guarantees.

closing.title: Do not force the remaining patterns into the monitor
keyPoints: No commands are queued or replayed as request objects
No public restore operation makes a Memento necessary
Four simple transition gates need no State hierarchy
The three selected boundaries already have concrete jobs
closing.narration: A capstone is not a checklist of every pattern name learned so far. This monitor does not need Command merely because it has methods, or Memento merely because it copies a vector. It does not need a State hierarchy merely because the enum is named State. Those patterns solve particular pressures such as storing requests, restoring snapshots through a caretaker, or delegating substantial state-specific behavior. Our program has different, smaller needs. Explain why the selected Adapter responsibility, Strategy operation, and Facade request are useful, then state why the alternatives are unnecessary today. Choosing less structure with a clear argument is a sign of understanding, not an incomplete design.

question.prompt: Would naming the staging vector “memento” establish the Memento pattern?
question.answer: No. A name does not create the pattern’s roles or intent. Here the vector is a private transaction candidate and there is no snapshot restore interface or caretaker relationship.

closing.title: Defend the next feature before changing code
keyPoints: New units belong at the conversion boundary
New decisions belong behind AlertRule
New presentation belongs at the reporting boundary
Ordering, state, capacity, and atomicity need broader review
closing.narration: Consider four proposed changes. A new external unit first affects adaptation and its validation tests. A new alert decision should fit AlertRule only if it can keep the existing nonthrowing, side-effect-free contract. A new display format can sit beside the report service while preserving the meaning of stored flags. A change to ordering, capacity, state gates, or all-or-nothing batches affects the monitor’s core contract and deserves broader review. This is the practical outcome of the course: identify what varies, locate its boundary, and defend the guarantees across that boundary. A useful design makes likely changes local while keeping the hard shared promises visible.

question.prompt: A proposed rule needs to send a network alert while judging each sample. Can it be added as an ordinary AlertRule implementation under the current contract?
question.answer: No. Its outside effect violates the side-effect-free rule contract and could survive a rejected batch. Design notification after a successful commit or define a wider transaction model.
